author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Diagnose frame pacing on a 120 Hz phone
summary: Compare fixed 60 Hz and 120 Hz at full emulation speed, separate recurring cadence from event-based stutter, and verify the chosen mode over a sustained thermal pass.
heroAlt: Smooth Criminal gameplay benchmark scene used for a sustained 60 Hz and 120 Hz frame-pacing comparison

sourceLabels.android-frame-pacing: Android display synchronization and frame-pacing concepts

blocks.text: Compare interval regularity, not the refresh label

Select a long camera pan or scrolling scene that holds full emulation speed. Lock the phone to 60 Hz, record frame-time data and video, then repeat at a fixed 120 Hz without changing resolution, renderer, or game state. Disable automatic refresh switching for the comparison and note whether Android actually applies the requested mode while EmuCoreX is in the foreground.

A 120 Hz badge and a high average FPS do not prove even presentation. Short interval spikes can remain visible while the average looks perfect, and some phones alternate refresh policy according to touch or brightness. Do not mix shader-cache warm-up, thermal drift, and display-mode changes in the same run.

items: Phone exposes fixed 60 Hz and 120 Hz modes for comparison.
Scene runs without compilation or loading events after warm-up.
Performance overlay or slow-motion capture available.
Record Android's observed refresh mode, a warmed frame-time trace, thermal state, and the same camera pan at fixed 60 Hz before 120 Hz.
Use a scene without loading or new shader work so interval changes track display scheduling rather than first-run compilation.

blocks.text: Challenge both high-refresh cadence and stability

items: 1. Warm the scene once so first-run shader events are excluded.
2. Run a fixed 60 Hz pass and record recurring judder positions.
3. Run a fixed 120 Hz pass with identical emulator settings.
4. Compare interval regularity instead of only average frame rate.
5. Repeat a known loading event to distinguish event-based stutter.
6. Observe whether Android changes refresh mode automatically during menus or video.
7. Continue each pass long enough to expose thermal performance loss.
8. Keep the mode that remains regular, not merely the one with the highest label.

blocks.text: A hitch at the same asset or effect may be shader compilation or storage; a repeating cadence across a clean pan points to scheduling or refresh interaction. Compare cold and warmed runs, inspect emulation speed, and align the frame-time trace with the recording. If 60 Hz is even but 120 Hz oscillates, the display path is implicated rather than game logic.

Run each fixed mode for several minutes, including one background/resume cycle, and verify that Android does not silently switch modes. The chosen mode passes when frame intervals remain consistent after warm-up and motion does not develop periodic judder. Preserve raw frame-time samples, not only an FPS counter screenshot.

items: Warm repeated passes exclude first-run compilation events.
The selected mode has regular motion and stable refresh behavior.
Long-session performance remains full speed without cadence collapse.
Overlay both traces and mark periodic cadence, isolated hitches, and any silent refresh switch; an average FPS value is not sufficient evidence.
Relaunch at the chosen fixed mode and run the pan for several minutes, including background and resume, without refresh-policy oscillation.
Both modes hitch at one loading point: investigate storage or compilation.
Only long runs degrade: diagnose thermal throttling.
Refresh switches in menus: use a stable supported mode for testing.
Frame times are regular but the game camera steps: preserve the title's native behavior.

blocks.text: Return to the prior phone refresh setting

Restore the user's refresh policy and remove the temporary per-app display override. Relaunch the game and confirm the system returns to the original mode. Leave renderer, speed controls, and game patches at their recorded baseline so the display experiment can be reversed without creating a second timing problem.
High refresh can display repeated frames cleanly or unevenly

A 120 Hz panel supplies more presentation slots, but smooth output still depends on emulator cadence, Android's compositor, and the game's native frame pattern. Some 30 fps titles will not become fluid merely by doubling panel refresh. Report requested and observed refresh, frame-time distribution, thermal state, and whether the run was cold or warmed.
